subject: seahorse
pitch: A lined seahorse holding on to a strand of seagrass with its curled tail. A ridged body in sunny yellow with thin dark lines and a few white freckles, a little crown of spikes on its head, a long tube snout, a delicate fluttering fin on its back, and big, curious eyes.
reasoning:
I'm sketching proportions for a realistic seahorse model—about 15cm tall, curled near a taller seagrass strand rooted in a small sand mound, with the tail wrapping around the grass for support.

I'm plotting the body's spine curve from head to tail in coordinate space, placing the head, neck, chest, belly, and trunk points, then working out how the tail should curl around the grass stem since real seahorse tails grip sideways rather than curling in the same plane as the body.

I'll make the grass a vertical blade and have the tail wrap around it as a shrinking helix, descending along the y-axis with a small pitch and radius that tapers down to match the grass stem's thickness.

I'll accept a slight bend where the tail transitions into the helix, letting the sweep's corner rounding smooth it out, then let the helix curl around the axis with its downward pitch before settling into the final chain with roughly 14 joints for the sweep.

For the grass, I'll keep its axis mostly straight near the base and curving gently from the floor up to height 0.4, with the seahorse's tail hovering a bit above it so the overall composition reads naturally.

I also need ground elements—a small sand mound at the base with pebbles, sinking slightly so grass starts just above it. For the body, I should plan the joint chain from head through neck to tail, keeping the spine joints as one role group and the tail joints as a separate role.

Now I'm figuring out how to split the body into trunk and tail sections sharing a single path: define a full catmull-rom path, find where the core joint sits along it, then slice forward and backward from that point to get front and back halves, reversing the segment as needed so the tail tip is t=0 and the head is t=1.

Still slicing the trunk and tail chains...

For the rest I'm mapping out radius growth along the tail toward the trunk, then narrowing through the neck, and thinking about using elliptical cross-sections since a seahorse is laterally compressed -- wider front-to-back than side-to-side at the belly, tapering differently near the tail.

Now I'm thinking through how to add the characteristic ridged texture: faceted hexagonal cross-sections for the ridge look, plus custom banding using periodic dark stripes based on position along the path, and layering in freckle-like spots using cell noise for a mottled pattern.

I'm trying to figure out which side of the curved body counts as the "back" for placing dorsal spikes, reasoning through the tangent and perpendicular directions along the path to pick a consistent back-facing normal.

I'll place spikes using the cone part aimed backward with radius based on the depth function, computing each position as the surface point offset along the back vector scaled by the body's depth at that spot. For the ridges, I'll skip explicit rings and rely on the faceted ngon shape plus paint for texture, then start laying out the seahorse's path coordinates from head through curved neck, puffed chest, belly, and curling tail.

Now I'm refining that curve, placing tail start, belly, chest, neck, and neck-top points with slight z-offsets to give the S-shape its characteristic curve, then positioning the head joint pitched forward and down at roughly 25 degrees for the snout.

I'm sizing the snout as a tapered tube and the skull as a small sphere, checking overall proportions against a real lined seahorse, then adding stylized oversized eyes with amber outer spheres, dark pupils, and a white glint for highlight.

Now I'm planning the coronet spikes as a ring of small cones atop the head plus a pair of cheek spines, and setting up the head/jaw joint hierarchy with the upper snout swept along the head direction.

I'm computing the snout geometry: a tapered rod from skull to snout tip forming the upper jaw, a shorter thinner rod for the lower jaw hinged near the tip, and placing the mouth opening at the snout's end, working out exact coordinates using the normalized head direction vector.

I'll add a dark sphere inside the mouth tip for depth, skip nostrils, and give small brow spine cones over the eyes. For the dorsal fin, I'm planning a fluttering membrane along the back at mid-trunk using two offset edge lines with connecting rays.

Now I'm extruding the fin as a thin flat panel in the YZ plane, positioned at the back of the body, matching the outline to the body's back curve coordinates along y and z.

Still shaping fin outline points...

I'm adjusting the root points to embed deeper into the body, then plotting out the full outline sequence for the fin shape, checking it stays non-self-intersecting and roughly convex. Now I need to think about how the fin attaches to the nearest bone joint so it can flutter naturally.

For the dorsal fin, I'm giving it its own joint under the trunk core, and adding a radial ray pattern using an angle-based paint function so the fin shows amber rays against a pale cream-yellow base, computed from the extruded point coordinates. I'm also planning small pectoral fins just behind the head on either side.

Working out pectoral fin placement...

Now I'm thinking through the brood pouch bulge for the male seahorse's belly, and planning the dark painted rings spaced along the body, estimating path length through the neck and helical tail turns to space them evenly.

I'll derive the ring count from the actual computed body length rather than hardcoding a frequency, and I'm also considering adding faceted ridge geometry using a hexagonal cross-section for a more angular, textured look along the tail.

For the radius profile, I'm setting up an interpolation helper that takes key points along the parameter t and blends between them, with the tail tapering from a thin tip near the body to a wider base before narrowing again toward the trunk.

Still defining radius keys...

Checking the pitch and turns for the tail helix — with radius 0.008 and pitch 0.022 the wraps won't overlap, so the descent from y=0.115 down to 0.078 works cleanly. Now I'm setting up the spiral parameters: center, start point, and downward axis to define how the tail coils around.

Defining more joints...

Still positioning the jaw...

I'm defining radius keys at each landmark point along the trunk—tail, lower, belly, chest, neck—interpolating smoothly between them so the tube cross-section widens through the belly/chest and narrows again toward the neck before the head takes over.

I'm sizing the joint chain: 14 segments for the tail helix, 3 for the trunk, 3 for the neck, roughly 23 total. Adding more blade curves...
